profile.summary: Enformer is a neural network that predicts gene expression and other genomic signals directly from DNA sequence. It reads about 200 kb of sequence and predicts 5,313 human (or 1,643 mouse) tracks, such as CAGE, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq signal, in 128 bp bins across the central 114,688 bp. Comparing predictions for reference and alternate sequences gives variant effect scores, and precomputed scores are published for common 1000 Genomes variants.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Enformer is a supervised model trained to reproduce measured genomic tracks. It has three parts: seven convolutional blocks with pooling that reduce 196,608 bp to 1,536 positions of 128 bp each, eleven transformer blocks that let distant positions exchange information, and a cropping layer followed by pointwise convolutions into separate human and mouse output heads. The transformer layers use relative positional basis functions and give a receptive field that reaches elements up to 100 kb away. It was trained jointly on human and mouse data from the Basenji2 dataset, with the input extended to 196,608 bp.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and Training; Results

quotes.text: The Enformer architecture consists of three parts: (1) 7 convolutional blocks with pooling, (2) 11 transformer blocks, and (3) a cropping layer followed by final pointwise convolutions branching into 2 organism-specific network heads
The convolutional blocks with pooling first reduce the spatial dimension from 196,608 bp to 1,536 so that each sequence position vector represents 128 bp
Enformer uses custom relative positional basis functions in the transformer layers
reaching distal regulatory elements up to 100 kb away while still being able to effectively integrate their information
We modified the Basenji2 dataset by extending the input sequence to 196,608 bp from the original 131,072 bp using the hg38 reference genome.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pre-trained model is published, at https://tfhub.dev/deepmind/enformer/1, with code to load its weights into the Sonnet Enformer module for fine-tuning. The README's inference example passes 393,216 bp, of which the model uses only the central 196,608 bp. Precomputed SAD and SAR variant scores on hg19 and their top 20 principal components are published for frequent 1000 Genomes variants. The paper also describes fine-tuning the model on human data. A result should state the model URL and version, whether published scores were used, and the genome build.

run_guide.summary: Get the Enformer code, install its pinned requirements, run the unit test, then load the pre-trained model from TF Hub and predict tracks for one all-zero input.
prerequisites: Python 3.8, as in the README's test instructions, and the pinned packages in requirements.txt (TensorFlow 2.5.0, dm-sonnet 2.0.0, tensorflow-hub 0.11.0).
The usage notebook asks for a GPU; memory needs are not stated.
Network access to tfhub.dev for the weights.
Code is Apache-2.0; no weights licence is stated.

steps.title: Load the pre-trained model and predict
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow_hub as hub

enformer = hub.load('https://tfhub.dev/deepmind/enformer/1').model

SEQ_LENGTH = 393_216
inputs = tf.zeros((1, SEQ_LENGTH, 4), dtype=tf.float32)
predictions = enformer.predict_on_batch(inputs)
print(predictions['human'].shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's inference example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. The model is loaded with hub.load(...).model as in the usage notebook instead of the README's hub.Module line, and a print is added. A real input is a one-hot encoded sequence of the same length.

The official code lives in a monorepo folder; the paper links github.com/deepmind/deepmind-research, and on 2026-11-26 the GitHub API resolved that name to google-deepmind/deepmind-research, which is where the files were fetched. On 2026-11-26 a GET of https://tfhub.dev/deepmind/enformer/1 redirected to the Kaggle model page https://www.kaggle.com/models/deepmind/enformer/tensorFlow2/enformer/1, so the weights now sit on Kaggle; that page was not saved and its licence was not read.
